subject: Spatial field confounded with predictor variables

messages.author: c0c2ba9b15004cad
messages.subject: Spatial field confounded with predictor variables
parts:
Greetings and thank you in advance for advice. 

I am asking the research question "Are there less birds along portions of the coast that are more degraded?"

My data is a long-term set of observations describing bird counts at ~25 sections of coastline along 1000 miles of a coast the runs primarily north to south. Observations were often repeated at the same sections of coastline (exact locations varied slightly within these coastal sections) over many years. Simple data exploration suggests that there are less birds along sections of the coast that are more degraded.  

The variables are: 
Response: Bird presence (and bird counts when present)
Spatial index: Latitude
Temporal index: Year
Covariates: Day of year (abundances peak in spring/summer); DegraderPC1 (higher = more degraded); DegraderPC2 (higher = more degraded).

The data is zero inflated and am fitting a binomial model on presence/absence data and a negative binomial model when birds are present (i.e., a hurdle model). For brevity, I will discuss here only the binomial model component, which is essentially parameterized the same as the negative binomial model. 

DegraderPC1 and DegraderPC2 are orthogonal principal components describing types of habitat degradation. Even though the data has been collected for 25 years, we have only one measure of DegraderPC1 and DegraderPC2 for each section of coast, and thus for every observation at that section of coast assume the same DegraderPC1 and DegraderPC2 values (i.e., we assume that that coastal section has maintained the same level of degradation for the entire time series).

My approach was to:
(1) fit a one dimensional mesh to the data based on the latitude of the observations, (one dimension rather than two since I am describing an essentially linear range of habitat (a coast the runs north to south)),  
(2) allow the spatial field to vary year-to-year according to an AR1 process,
(3) treat day of year as a RW2 process to allow abundances to peak in the spring/summer,
and (4) estimate parameters for my main (fixed) effects of interest: DegraderPC1 and DegraderPC2, which I anticipate to be negative. 

The basic code is thus: 
  
meshBird<-inla.mesh.1d(as.matrix(Bird$Latitude))
spdeBird<-inla.spde2.matern(meshBird)
A.Bird<-
  inla.spde.make.A(meshBird,
                   loc=as.matrix(Bird$Latitude),
                   group=Bird$Year,
                   n.group = 25) #25 years in the dataset
field.indiciesBird<-inla.spde.make.index("field",n.spde=meshBird$n,n.group=25)
stack.Bird=
  inla.stack(
    data=list(Presence.Absence=Bird$Presence.Absence),
    A=list(A.Bird,1),
    effects=list(c(field.indiciesBird,
                   list(Intercept=1)),
                 list(data.frame(
                   DegraderPC1=Bird$DegraderPC1,
                   DegraderPC2=Bird$DegraderPC2,
                   day.of.year=Bird$day.of.year,
                   Year=Bird$Year))))
formulaBird<-Presence.Absence ~ -1 + Intercept  + DegraderPC1 + DegraderPC2 + 
  f(field,model=spdeBird,group=field.group,control.group=list(model="ar1"))+
  f(day.of.year,model="rw2"))
modBird<-inla(formulaBird,
                 data=inla.stack.data(stack.Bird,spde=Bird),
                 family="binomial",
                 control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.Bird),
                                          compute=TRUE))
summary(modBird)

The problem is that I am getting positive parameter estimates for the DegraderPCs (i.e., the model says that there are more birds along coasts that are more degraded), which is the opposite of what simple data exploration shows and is counterintuitive. When I examine estimates for the spatial field (i.e., how does bird presence vary by latitude?) it shows a pattern that is virtually the opposite of how DegraderPC1 varies with latitude. In other words, the model appears to be attributing low presence of birds at degraded sections of coast due to a spatial effect rather than because that section of coast is more degraded, and then as an artifact estimates birds to be more likely to be present at more degraded sections of coast. Unfortunately, there is a pattern that portions of the coast at the northern and southern ends of my spatial range are more degraded, so I'm not sure whether increasing the smoothing of the spatial field will resolve this.   

My question is, is there any way to resolve this while addressing the spatiotemporal structure in my dataset? That is, I want my analysis to account for the premise that observations at proximate sections of coast (and years) will be similar. The alternative seems to be to ignore the spatial component and refit the model treating the sections of coast as iid models, and acknowledge the caveat of spatial non-independence this in the paper. 

Again, thank you very much for the help.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial field confounded with predictor variables
parts:
To deal with such spatial confounding, I suggest two things:
1) be more careful with the priors. Currently you're not explicitly specifying the field parameter priors at all. I also suggest looking at inla.spde2.pcmatern for a better prior distribution model.
2) impose integration constraints on the field model. constr=TRUE in
inla.spde2.(pc)matern imposes an integrate-to-zero constraint, but you can also
impose orthogonal-to-covariates constraints via either extraconstr or extraconstr.int where the latter gives integral constrains, like
\int field(s) covariate(s) ds = 0

Finn
